“We have captured 598 camps. Until last night, their aircraft dropped about 53 bombs. This morning, we have cleared the camps. We have not yet received a detailed list of the weapons and equipment that were damaged,” the joint secretary of Khle Lwe Htoo (Nyaung Lay Bin) district confirmed to KIC.

At the same time, a reliable KNLA source confirmed that the KNLA and the joint forces have also captured Hte Khi camp on the Thai-Myanmar border, which is under attack by the joint forces.

“We captured the Htei Khe camp at around 9am this morning. We cannot give any further details,” said a KNLA Brigade (4) source.

The camp has been under siege by the KNLA for three weeks, and the offensive has led to the escape of nearly half of the 100 MMK soldiers based in the camp to Thailand. The KIC is still in contact with the Secretary of the Beit-Tawei District, Padoh Saw Aen Na, for information on the weapons and ammunition seized after the camp was captured. 

Similarly, the MMK Brigade (7) launched an attack on the camp on March 7, and the KNLA and the joint forces have also completely captured and cleared the Takhor Bhikhe camp, which is based on the MMK Infantry Battalion, Battalion-24, Company-1, in Paing Kyung Township, Hpa-an District, this morning, according to a military source.

While the KNLA was attacking the camp, the military council launched airstrikes, forcing the locals to flee to the Thai side and nearby safe havens.

This year, military council camps in KNU-controlled areas have been attacked by the KNLA joint forces, and most recently on April 19, the joint forces captured the military council’s Htet Hta strategic camp in Brigade (4) and the Lay Gow (Mawgla) camp in Brigade (7) Nabu Township in a single day.

KNU says it cleared Ta Khor Bekwe camp as it affected local livelihoods

May 9, 2025. KIC 

The Karen National Union-KNU-controlled area, Brigade (7), Hpa-an District, has attacked and cleared the Ta Khor Bekwe (aka Lay Pana Di) camp as it could affect the livelihoods of local Karen people, the KNU said.

The Ta Khor Bekwe camp in Paikyong Township, where the 24th Infantry Battalion of the Military Council is based, was completely captured by the Karen National Liberation Army-KNLA, Karen National Defense Force-KNDO and joint forces on the morning of May 9.

The camp, which has been stationed in the area of ​​the 7th Brigade for around 30 years, was attacked and cleared because it could affect the livelihood of the local Karen people, said Brigadier General Saw Dikwe Htoo, commander of the 7th Brigade.

“We, the Karen people, live in this area. If the military camp is there, it will cause a lot of disruption and danger to our Karen people’s livelihood such as farming, mountaineering, and corn production. That is why we are working towards our ultimate goal that this area is Karen land and only Karens should rule it,” Brigadier General Saw Dikwe Htoo told KIC.

The KNLA joint forces have been conducting military operations at the Takhon Bekwe camp since May 7, and the battle to capture the camp lasted only 2 days. Thai sources also reported that more than 300 locals around the camp fled to Tha Saung Yang Township, Thailand, during the fighting.

The KNU has not yet released the details of the weapons and ammunition seized in the camp capture battle and the casualties on both sides.

The KNLA joint forces have since captured the Lay Gow (Mawgla) camp in Nabu Township, Khle Dey camp in Hlaing Bwe Township, and Pulutu camp in Paing Kyaw Township, all of which were military council posts within the 7th Brigade area, from March to April 2025. In addition to the Takhor Bekwe camp, the 4th Brigade also captured the Htee Khee camp and the 598th Brigade camp in the 3rd Brigade this morning.

LBC Battalion Appeals for Support as Medical Center Builds for Frontline Comrades

May 10, 2025. KIC 

The Lion Battalion Commando is appealing for support from the public as it begins construction of a health care center to provide medical care to wounded comrades on the frontline in the KNU-Karen National Organization, Brigade (6) area.

The center is being built by the Battalion Commander, Major Al Say Wah, and aims to provide mental and physical health care and rehabilitation to revolutionary comrades who have been injured or lost limbs in the fighting, said a comrade from the Lion Battalion Commando Strategic Battalion.

“Comrades on the front lines can’t rest. The military council is bombing our base in various ways, both with artillery and aircraft, so it’s not comfortable in the front. That’s why we built this care center so that we can get medical treatment in the back comfortably,” he told KIC. 

The center, named “Heaven of Relief Care Center,” is already under construction and needs medicine and equipment, he added. He added that the lives and injuries of the comrades are in great need of help from the people. 

The campaign period for the center’s construction is set from March 18 to June 18 this year, and the expected amount is 300,000 Thai baht (4,500,000 kyats), but so far, only 480,000 baht has been donated, a military official said. 

In addition, those who want to help can connect with the Lion Battalion Commando military headquarters through the Heaven of Relief social network page and contribute through Thai or Myanmar Banking Payment, the military commander informed. 

In addition, the Lion Battalion Commando military headquarters is also conducting a “Wild King Campaign” to increase the number of weapons and ammunition to carry out urban battles more effectively, and is inviting people to contribute to meet the requirements.

KNU says it is taking back control of Htet Khe base to ensure the security of both countries

May 10, 2025. KIC 

The KNU-4th Brigade issued a letter to the people along the Htet Khe border on the night of May 9, saying it was taking back control of the military council’s Htet Khe base to ensure the security of both Thai and Myanmar local people. 

The KNU-4th Brigade issued a letter to the Thai people in Thai-Burmese-English in order to regain control of the Htet Khe base, which has been under military control for 28 years. 

The appeal letter from the 4th Brigade stated that they have thoroughly analyzed the potential harm and its consequences due to the military tension between the KNU and the military council, and have made every effort to minimize the harm. 

The KNU also stated that they have lived in harmony with the Thai people in the past and present, and they promise to live in good neighborly friendship in the future. 

In addition, the KNU said that the news that the military council will build a 110-megawatt nuclear power plant using Russian technology in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in Tanintharyi Region and in the central Bago region on the Thai border has raised concerns among the people living in the border areas for security, safety and a good quality of life. 

The KNU said that military action is needed against the military council to give the people the right to create their own destiny and to free themselves from the violence of the Burmese army.

The KNU Myeik-Dawei district also issued a statement to honor all those who supported the allied revolutionary forces who fought bravely with the KNU/KNLA Brigade (4) in the battle to capture the military council camp on the Htee Khee border, and all those who provided technical and financial support to achieve victory, and those who sent prayers and wishes for the safety of the fighting comrades. 

After the military council camp in the area was captured by the KNLA Brigade (4) and allied revolutionary forces on April 19, the military council carried out heavy airstrikes on the Htee Khee border, forcing local residents to flee to the Thai border.

Funds raised from event to continue to help displaced people in Dooplaya district

May 11, 2025. KIC 

The organizers of the event, which was held on May 10, will continue to use the funds raised from the fundraising event for displaced people in Dooplaya district due to the recent fighting and airstrikes. 

The fundraiser, titled Together for Dooplaya, was held yesterday evening at Parami School in Mae Sot, on the Thai-Myanmar border, led by the Karen Student Association -Chaing Mai University and the Karen Youth Group in Mae Sot. 

“We are currently tallying the funds raised from yesterday’s event. The participating shops will also contribute funds, so we don’t know how much we will get. We are continuing to help those displaced by the fighting as soon as possible,” said Man Bwa, one of the organizers.

Organizers said the event was organized because many villagers are currently displaced due to the military council’s aerial bombing and artillery shelling in Kyando-Kawkareik townships in Duplaya district and are in need of various kinds of assistance. 

Naw Joe Thalay, who participated in the fundraiser, said, “I am happy to be able to attend and help as this is a fundraiser to help displaced people. The main part of the event is selling food. I want to encourage the displaced people that no matter how they are displaced, Karen people like us will help them as much as we can.” 

The fundraiser held yesterday evening included a football tournament, a food and clothing market, and a music concert, and most of the young people who had arrived in Mae Sot participated.

New IDPs Arrive in Mae La Hta, Thailand

May 12, 2025. KIC 

The Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) and the Karen National Defense Army (KNDO) are attacking the KNU’s Ta Leh Military Council camp in Pa Kyung Township, Hpa-an District, and new IDPs arrived in Mae La Hta village, Tha Song Yang Township, Thailand on May 10, according to a villager. 

The Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) and the Karen National Defense Army (KNDO) were able to completely capture the Ta Khor Bek Kwee (Ley Pan Di) camp in Pa Kyung Township, Pa Kyung Township, on May 9, so more than 250 IDPs who fled to Thailand returned home on May 10. 

However, a local Thai Karen said that new refugees arrived in Mae La Hta, Tha Song Yang Township, Thailand on May 10 as the junta continued to attack the military council’s Ta Le strategic camp in Pa Kyung Township. 

“Some have returned and some are still here. On the Thai side, there are two places at Mae La Hta Monastery and Mae Ao Pha Lu Monastery. The refugees in Mae Ao Pha Lu all left yesterday. I think we will send some back today in Mae La Hta. First, I will ask if they have been able to return or not,” he told KIC. 

He added that humanitarian NGOs in Thailand are helping the refugees who have crossed into Thailand. 

In addition, the Bangkok Post, a Thai news outlet, reported that more than 300 people fled to Thailand on May 10 due to fighting between the KNLA and the military council. 

During the current 2025, the KNU has successively seized the military council-occupied KNU camps in Paing Kyaw Township, Ta Khow Be Kwee and Pu Lu Tu, the Khle Dae camp in Hlaing Bwe Township, and the Lay Waw (Maw Klar) camp in Nabu Township.

JFM calls for blocking the flow of military support to the military council through ASEAN member states

May 13, 2025. KIC 

Justice For Myanmar-JFM yesterday, May 13, called on ASEAN to impose a blockade on the flow of military support, such as finance, technology and aviation fuel, to the military council through ASEAN member states.

JFM called for the “ASEAN List of 30+ Corrupt Persons” who benefit from the financial support, sale of military equipment and services linked to the military regime’s business activities that are based on the violence against the Burmese people.

ASEAN has adopted five common understandings but has not taken action, and military equipment, including weapons, is being allowed to flow to the military council, JFM spokesperson Ma Yadana Maung said in a statement.

“For four years, ASEAN has failed the people of Burma. On the one hand, a wealthy group of government officials has allowed weapons and military equipment to flow into the hands of war criminals. There is always a business connection to every airstrike by the military junta, and these business elites must be held accountable,” said Ma Yadana Maung.

JFM’s “ASEAN 30+ Corruption List” details the connections between the military council, which includes 12 individuals from Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore, who are influential in Southeast Asia.

JFM also pointed out that ASEAN member states are complicit in the war crimes committed by the military council by allowing money to flow to and arms from businesses owned by these individuals under their jurisdiction.

On the same day that the statement was released, the military council The National Unity Government (NUG) said it had dropped two cluster bombs on a school in Oh Htein Kwin village in Depayin Township. The bombs killed 22 teachers and students who were taking exams and injured more than 40.

According to JFM, the military council has carried out more than 500 air and artillery strikes across the country, including in areas affected by the earthquake, since the coup and the devastating earthquake centered in Sagaing earlier this year.

KNLA joint forces capture Ta Le strategic camp, seize large quantities of ammunition including artillery shells

May 14, 2025. KIC 

The Karen National Liberation Army-KNLA joint forces captured the Ta Le strategic camp of the Karen National Union-KNU, Brigade (7), in Hpa-an District, yesterday evening, and captured a large quantity of ammunition including 120 mm artillery shells.

The KNLA joint forces captured the Ta Le strategic camp, located near the Thai-Myanmar border in Paing Kyaw Township, Hpa-an District, after a five-day battle to capture the camp.

After capturing the camp, the Karen National Union-KNU, 120 mm, A KNLA official from Brigade (7) who participated in the battle told KIC that the KNLA joint forces had captured more than 30 pieces of ammunition and weapons, including many 81mm shells.

The commander said, “Our situation is good. We have a lot of ammunition. We have a lot of 120mm shells and 81mm shells. If we count the 120 shells, that’s over 70. We have over 30 pieces of weapons. We haven’t even counted them yet.”

After capturing the Tale strategic camp, which had a force of over 40 MMK soldiers, the KNLA found 11 MMK soldiers dead during the clearing operation, and over 20 MMK soldiers had fled the camp, according to a KNLA source.

The commander, who participated in the battle, continued, “We know that there are 45 people in the camp. There are no survivors. When they could no longer resist, they all fled. We know that there are over 20 who fled.”

In addition, Thai sources reported on social media that the KNLA coalition attacked the military council base, which is only 7 kilometers from the Thai border, and the military council provided air support, but was unable to resist and had to retreat from the base.

The military launched at least 4 airstrikes on the base this morning after it was taken over. Also, since the attack began, villagers from the surrounding villages have been fleeing to Mae La Hta in Tha Song Yang Township, Thailand, and Thai authorities have provided assistance, according to locals on the Thai side.

The KNLA coalition also seized the Takho Bik Kwee (Lae Pana Di) base in Pai Kyung Township on May 9, as part of the KNU Brigade (7) designation.

BGF transfers over 400 illegal gambling workers in two days

May 14, 2025. KIC 

The Border Guard Force (BGF) has transferred 425 more foreigners who were involved in online gambling in Myawaddy Township to Thai authorities via the Thai-Myanmar Friendship Bridge No. 2 on May 13 and 14.

A total of 425 people, including (211) Vietnamese nationals, (35) Pakistani nationals, (1) South African nationals and (178) Ethiopian nationals, including a pregnant woman, were transferred to their respective countries through Thai government officials in the past two days, a BGF source said.

The BGF has repeatedly denied involvement in illegal gambling operations operating in its territory and continues to deport foreigners. However, it has not escaped pressure from neighboring Thailand and China, and was also subject to sanctions from the United States on May 5.

In the nearly four months since the start of the crackdown on human trafficking and smuggling, the BGF has reportedly detained more than 8,000 foreigners. Of these, more than 7,000 have been transferred, leaving just over 1,000 foreigners to be deported, he said at a press conference on April 28.

KNU releases statement on arrest of 2nd Battalion Commander and his team who fled from Tale camp

May 15, 2025. KIC

KNU-Karen National Union, Brigade (7) in Paing Kyaw Township, Hpa-an District, announced today that the 24th Battalion Commander and his team of the 24th Infantry Battalion of the 24th Infantry Battalion of the 24th Infantry Battalion of the 24th Infantry Battalion of the 31 The KNU statement said that nine people, including an officer from the 311th Military Council, were killed in the fighting, and that the KNLA joint forces were pursuing the escaped military council members and a deputy commander from the 24th Battalion.

A commander of the 7th Brigade of the KNLA who was fighting told KIC yesterday that more than 20 military council members had fled the camp.

The military council has been stationed in the camp in KNU territory since 1986, and the local residents in the vicinity have lost their right to move freely, the KNU statement said.

“We must clear all enemy troops in our territory. We do not want them in our territory. Because they are causing inconvenience and obstruction to the movement of civilians, we must clear them all,” a commander of the 7th Brigade of the KNLA said yesterday regarding the battle to capture the Tale camp.

In addition, the KNLA said it had seized a large number of artillery shells and other weapons from the military council during the camp capture battle.

The KNLA has been continuously attacking military council camps throughout the first half of this year, and in the battle to capture the camp of Brigade (4) on the Thai-Myanmar border, which was captured a few days ago, more than 40 military council soldiers fled to Thailand.

Over 400 IDPs Cross Border into Thailand Due to Fighting Over Border Military Camp

May 15, 2025. KIC 

Thai media reports that 414 local IDPs have crossed into Tha Song Yang Township, Thailand, due to fighting in Mae La Camp, a military base of the KNU-Karen National Union, Brigade (7) Control Area, Hpa-an District, Thailand-Myanmar Border Military Council.

Starting from the night of May 14, some local IDPs said that the Karen National Liberation Army-KNLA joint forces have begun attacking the military council camp in Paikyong Township.

Most of the IDPs include women and children, and Thai authorities have provided temporary shelters in Mae La Sub-Township, Tha Song Yang Township, according to Thai sources.

“The camp is close to the village and is now on the Thai side. We were still in the village until last night. We crossed over to the Thai side this morning. Other villages have been on the move since before the capture of Ta Le. Now, we have probably only left four or five villages on this side. When we got to the Thai side, some of them are staying in their homes,” a displaced woman told KIC this afternoon.

The Thai authorities have allocated two separate areas for the displaced, and the relevant Thai troops are monitoring the situation at the border.

In May, the KNLA joint forces captured the Ta Khor Bik Kwee camp and Ta Le camp along the Thai-Myanmar border in the 7th Brigade area, Pa Kyung Township. Thai news reports indicate that during the camp-taking battles, villages near the camps repeatedly fled to the Thai side due to the military council’s airstrikes.

Blood Money Campaign Calls on International Organizations to Stop Funding Military Council for Effective Humanitarian Aid

May 15, 2025. KIC 

The Blood Money Campaign on May 13 called on international organizations to stop funding the Military Council to ensure that emergency aid and humanitarian assistance reach those in real need.

The Military Council has been hoarding and mishandling international food, medicine, and emergency supplies to earthquake victims in warehouses in Nay Pyi Taw, and continuing to fund them will not effectively reach those in real need, the Blood Money Campaign said.

Ma May, a spokesperson for the Blood Money Campaign, commented that international organizations should not continue to work with the Military Council in light of the control and profiteering of international humanitarian aid.

“The international community should provide assistance to the earthquake-stricken areas and people if they can. If they cannot, then they should not distribute it through the military junta, but through NUG, EROs, CSOs, CBOs. Work together. This is the only way to truly reach all the earthquake-stricken people,” he said.

In addition, the statement said that in the liberated areas, there was no access to aid at all because the military council restricted access, and that international humanitarian aid and money were being placed in the hands of organizations under their control, preventing aid from reaching those in need.

“Currently, this group is also able to connect with local groups and deliver directly to the earthquake-affected areas and people. There are political forces, revolutionary forces, and civil society organizations that are working in this way. It reaches the people directly through this channel,” said Ma May, spokesperson for the Blood Money Campaign.

The military council, which has a long history of blocking, misusing, and using humanitarian aid as a weapon for military and political purposes, is still experiencing this today, according to the Blood Money Campaign.

The military junta illegally confiscated international aid supplies, including 38 tons of high-nutrient biscuits provided by the United Nations World Food Programme (UN WFP), after Cyclone Nargis in 2008, and also obstructed the delivery of aid, especially in Rakhine State, after Cyclone Mocha in 2023, according to the Blood Money Campaign statement.

Relief and relief supplies have been sent from 20 countries, including Russia, China, Hong Kong, India, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, Bangladesh, UAE, Laos, Belarus, Indonesia, Putin, Philippines, Japan, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, and the United States, for the earthquake disaster in Myanmar.

Fortify Rights urges Malaysia to block jet fuel supplies to military council

May 16, 2025. KIC 

Fortify Rights, the rotating chairman of ASEAN, urged Malaysia to take urgent measures to block the sale of jet fuel to the Myanmar military council, in a statement dated May 14.

Fortify Rights issued a statement on the incident in which at least 22 students, including two teachers, were killed and more than 50 injured when the military council dropped an airstrike on a school in Otin Dwin village, Depayin Township, Sagaing Region on the morning of May 12.

The group pointed out that Malaysia should take urgent measures, such as cooperation within ASEAN countries, to prevent the flow of weapons and supplies, including jet fuel, to the military council to protect the Burmese people.

Ko Sai Akar, human rights investigator at Fortify Rights, said it is not enough to ignore the military council’s crimes and issue statements, but to take immediate action.

“The failure of ASEAN to take action while the Myanmar military council is killing its own people is not a matter of Asian tradition. Strong written statements will never stop the military council. ASEAN must take immediate action,” Ko Sai Akar said in a statement.

Fortify Rights also said that the ASEAN Chair should propose emergency measures that could include a ban on aviation fuel, arms and aid at the 46th ASEAN Summit to be held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on May 26-27.

The military council has said that using jet fuel currently available on the international market is endangering the lives of civilians in Burma and that attacking schools and other places that are not military targets could constitute war crimes.

Similarly, while the military council has denied the incident at the Otindwin village school, Fortify Rights has been able to verify the authenticity of the incident through interviews with witnesses who were at the scene and through documentary footage. The statement also contains details of their statements.

According to a statement issued on May 13 regarding the bombing of the Otindwin school by the National Unity Government (NUG), more than 2,600 airstrikes were carried out between May 2023 and May 2025, and 240 schools were destroyed.

Regarding the junta’s airstrikes, Justice for Myanmar also issued a statement on May 13 calling for sanctions against the military council for providing technology, money, and military support such as jet fuel to the military council through ASEAN countries.

KNLA Captures Maung Kyi Lu Base in Mae La, Almost All Military Council Members Flee

May 16, 2025. KIC 

The Karen National Union-KNU, Brigade (7), Hpa-an District, has captured the Maung Kyi Lu Military Council base near Mae La village, Paing Kyung Township, at 5 a.m. today, May 16, and almost all the military council members in the base have fled, according to a KNLA Brigade (7) source.

The base, located near the Thai-Myanmar border, was captured a day after the attack began, and more than 40 of the 50 military council members in the base fled with their weapons.

“The base has a strength of more than 40 to 50. More than 40 military council members have fled. It was captured in more than 5 hours,” a KNLA commander confirmed this morning.

Two MMRC soldiers were killed in the battle for the camp, and another MMRC soldier was injured in a KNLA drone attack, but fled with the group that fled the camp.

In addition, the KNLA joint forces captured the MMRC’s 120mm and 60mm artillery pieces, as well as other ammunition, according to a KNLA commander on the front line.

Since last April, the KNLA joint forces have captured five MMRC camps in the KNU Brigade (7) area, including Lay Gow, Pulu Tu, Lay Panad, Tale and now Maw Kyi Lu, located on the Thai-Myanmar border.

Over 200 IDPs Return to Thailand after Battle for Maung Kyi Lu Camp

May 17, 2025. KIC 

IDPs who have been in Thailand since May 15 due to the battle for the Maung Kyi Lu Military Council camp in Paing Kyaw Township, Hpa-an District, Karen National Union-KNU controlled area, Brigade (7), have returned to Thailand this morning, according to the IDPs.

According to Thai sources, 414 people have crossed the Thaung Rin River to escape the fighting at two monasteries in Mae La Sub-Township, Tha Song Yang Township, Tak Province, Thailand, as the military council’s Maung Kyi Lu camp is being attacked by the Karen National Liberation Army-KNLA joint forces.

After the KNLA finally captured the camp on May 16, more than 200 displaced people returned to their homes in a Thai monastery this morning, a displaced woman said.

“There are more than 200 in the monastery. There are also many children. We returned this morning. Those who are living outside (in the known houses) returned yesterday. The Thai side is organizing everything. Other groups have also come and donated,” the woman told KIC.

In addition to the Thai authorities, other donor groups, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), Save the Children, and Shoklo Malaria Research Unit (SMRU), have also donated food and school supplies for the displaced.

Over the past two months, the military council’s border outposts in the Dawna Mountains of Hpa-an District have been continuously captured by the KNLA, the Karen National Defense Force (KNDO), and other forces. Thai sources say that the airstrikes by the junta have forced locals to flee to Thailand during each battle.

In April and May, the KNLA captured the junta’s Maw Kyi Lu camp, as well as the camps of Tale Thar, Ta Khow Bek Kwee, Pulu Tu, Khle De, and Maw Pha Thu. According to the Committee for Internally Displaced Persons (CIDKP), there were nearly 30,000 internally displaced persons in Hpa-an district in March before the fighting.

KNU Central Advisor Colonel Saw Htoo Htoo Lay Dies of Cancer

May 18, 2025. KIC 

Colonel Saw Htoo Htoo Lay, the military and political advisor to the KNU-Karen National Union-Central, passed away at 10:20 PM Thai time on May 17 at his niece’s home in Mae Sot, Thailand, due to colon cancer, according to his relatives and friends.

Saw Htoo Htoo Lay, who was 78 years old at the time of his death, had served as the official advisor to the KNU-Central during the 14th Congress of the KNU held in 2012 until his death.

On his death, KNDO Commander-in-Chief Brigadier General Saw Shee Lay said, “Major Saw Htoo Htoo was an important figure. He was a leader who carried out many important tasks. He guided the youth to the point where he bowed his head. Therefore, his absence is a great loss for our organization.”

Saw Htoo Htoo, who first arrived in the KNU Brigade (6) controlled area in 1979 during the Karen Revolution and became a member of the KNLA. He was promoted to the rank of captain in 1980 and was jointly responsible for the Justice Department and the Defense Department of the KNDO.

He was then promoted to the rank of colonel in 1991 and was elected as General Secretary (2) at the 11th KNU Congress in 1995 and as General Secretary (1) at the (12th) and (13th) Congresses.

“He always encouraged us, the young people, when we met him. When we heard that, it really gave us strength. He gave his best to the Karen people while he was alive. We, the survivors, must continue to follow the good example he set,” Brigadier General Saw Shee Lay added. 

Colonel Saw Htoo Htoo was born on May 26, 1947 in Yangon, the eldest of three siblings. After graduating with a law degree from Yangon University, he worked as a judicial officer and was transferred to Hpa-an in 1977, and was survived by his wife and three daughters.

KNLA Joint Forces Continue Attack on Military Council’s Border Outpost Maw Po Kay

May 19, 2025. KIC 

The Karen National Liberation Army-KNLA joint forces have been continuing their attacks on the Maw Po Kay camp, which is the base of the 24th Infantry Battalion of the Military Council near the Thai-Myanmar border, since the afternoon of May 19, according to ground reports.

The joint forces, which include the KNLA and the Karen National Defense Force-KNDO, have been continuously attacking the border outposts in Paing Kyung Township, Hpa-an District, under the control of the Karen National Union-KNU Brigade (7) for three months, and finally captured the Maw Koy Lu camp of the Military Council on May 16.

The field source also said that the KNLA joint forces are also using drones to attack the Maw Po Kay camp, as in recent camp-taking battles.

KNU spokesman Pado Saw Kale Say said in response to a question from the People’s Daily on May 16 that the KNU is working to clear the military council camps in the area.

In addition, according to reports on social media by Thai media and some authorities, 217 people have been displaced by the fighting in Mae La sub-district, Thailand. Authorities are providing assistance to the displaced, most of whom are women and children.

The KNLA joint forces have already captured military council camps along the 7th Brigade border in the past month, including Maw Pha Thu, Tale, Takho Bik Kwe, Pulu Tu, Khle De, Maw Kyi Lu, and Lay Gow.

KNU Captures 8th Maw Po Kay Camp in 3 Months 

May 20, 2025. KIC 

The Karen National Liberation Army-KNLA led an attack on the Maw Po Kay camp in Paing Kyaw Township, KNU-Karen National Union, Brigade (7) area, on the evening of May 19, a commander on the ground confirmed. 

The Maw Po Kay camp is located in Paing Kyaw (Tak Lae) Township of KNU Brigade (7) and has a strength of just over 10 Maw Po Kay soldiers. The KNLA Brigade (7) captured it in about half a day on May 18. 

When the KNLA began attacking the camp, the Maw Po Kay soldiers inside the Maw Po Kay camp destroyed their weapons and fled, a commander on the ground said. 

“We were able to finish the attack last night. There were no planes coming. All the SKS in the camp fled and were never found again. I don’t know where they went. None of the weapons were left,” he told KIC.

In addition to the Maw Po Khe (Maw Po Kay) camp along the Thai-Burma border in the current KNU Brigade (7) area, the KNU has been able to capture eight military bases in three months, including Maw Pha Thu, Tale, Ta Khor Bek Kwe, Pulu Tu, Khle Dae, Maw Kyi Lu and Lay Gow.

At the time of the capture of the camp, local residents had to temporarily flee to Thailand, but after the capture of the camp, locals said that although they had to live in their homes, they had to be careful of the military council’s airstrikes.

In addition, since December 2024, the KNU Brigade (7) The Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) and Karen National Defense Army (KNDO) of Brigade (5) jointly attacked and captured the former KNU headquarters in Manelpalaw.

9 civilians killed in Tanintharyi in April

May 20, 2025. KIC 

Nine civilians were killed in Tanintharyi Region last April, according to a report by FE 5Tanintharyi, a research group.

The killings of civilians occurred when the military council troops entered the area and arrested and killed 6 local residents. The remaining 2 were killed without incident.

In addition, the FE5 Tanintharyi report stated that the revolutionary forces killed U Myint Lwin, a real estate broker from Thaung Phyu Phyu Kye village in Kawthaung Township, claiming to be a clearing operation.

In Tanintharyi, there were forced military service arrests at military council checkpoints in April, FE5 Tanintharyi reported that at least 232 local people were arrested as human shields during the military incursions into villages, and only 50 were released.

The Myanmar media community, which has been underrepresented in female leadership since before the coup, has seen 27 percent of female media workers lose their jobs, 57 percent lose their income, and face fewer job opportunities during the funding cuts and suspensions, the report says.

According to the report, part-time and freelance female journalists are more likely to experience stress due to income and job instability due to funding cuts, which is leading to health problems.

Therefore, donors and non-governmental organizations need to continue supporting Myanmar’s media during the coup, including providing mental health treatment and funding to improve the long-term development of the media, MWiM said.

MWiM also pointed out that policymakers should develop and implement policies to protect female media professionals from discrimination, sexual harassment, and abuse of power, as well as provide a complaint channel.

MWiM, which aims to promote equality, freedom and opportunities for Myanmar women journalists and address challenges, said it compiled the report using three research methods: quantitative surveys, individual interviews and interviewing of informants.

UN General Assembly approves resolution to suspend Russia from Human Rights Council
The UN General Assembly approved a resolution on April 7 to suspend Russia from the Geneva-based Human Rights Council.

The draft resolution “Suspension of Russia from the Human Rights Council” was adopted by 93 of the 193 members of the General Assembly, with 24 voting against. A total of 58 abstained and 8 abstained.

China voted against the resolution, which was pushed by the United States.

A two-thirds majority of member states, excluding abstentions, can suspend a country from the 47-member council. Libya was also suspended in 2011 after forces loyal to Muammar Gaddafi violently crushed protests.

The resolution, which specifically addresses reports of human rights abuses by Russia, states that it is “concerned about the ongoing human rights and humanitarian crisis in Ukraine.”

Russia is in the second year of its three-year term as a member of the Geneva-based Human Rights Council.

The General Assembly also adopted two other resolutions related to Russia’s “special military operation” in Ukraine that began on February 24.

The United States announced that it would suspend Russia’s membership after Ukraine accused Russian forces of “killing hundreds of civilians” in the streets of the Kiev suburb of Bucha. Russia denies attacking civilians in Ukraine.

China’s permanent representative to the UN, Zhang Jun, told the assembly before the vote on the draft resolution that it was not drafted “with a transparent attitude” and “did not follow the tradition of all member states handling negotiations with the broadest possible perspective and careful consideration.”

“Under these circumstances, the General Assembly’s hasty action will only force countries to choose sides, which will only exacerbate the division between member states and create greater opposition among them. It will only add fuel to the fire. It will not reduce the intensity of the conflict, and it will even reduce the level of peace talks,” said Zhang Jun, China’s permanent representative to the UN.

Handling the membership of the Human Rights Council in this way could be “a dangerous new precedent,” Zhang said, adding that it could lead to further confrontations in the human rights field, have a major impact on the UN governance system, and have far-reaching consequences.

“That is why China voted against this draft resolution,” he stressed.

“China believes that all countries should work together on the same line of thinking, only then can we create opportunities for peace and prospects for dialogue. ---
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on July 22 rejected Myanmar’s objection to the Gambia’s claim that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. All four grounds of objection were rejected.
The ICJ said it considered objections (1) and (4) raised by Myanmar together and rejected them. The 16 judges of the ICJ unanimously rejected Myanmar’s objection that Gambia filed the case on behalf of the OIC and that there was no dispute between Myanmar and Gambia over the Rohingya issue. The judge read that Gambia had clearly expressed its concern about the Rohingya issue and that it would address the issue at UN and OIC meetings, and that it had acted on its own initiative. The ICJ ruled that the decision was also subject to the right to receive financial assistance from a related organization. Similarly, the Gambia’s objection to the speech made by the Myanmar representative at the UN, the Gambia’s objection to the UN Fact Finding Mission report cited by the Gambia, and the letter submitted by the Gambia to the Myanmar Mission to the UN. The ICJ ruled that there was a specific dispute between the Gambia and Myanmar on this issue.
The ICJ also considered the third objection by the Myanmar side, which was that the Gambia did not have the right to use the ICJ as a single country because it had made an exception to Article 8 on genocide, and decided that the Gambia had the right to submit a case to the ICJ only on the basis of Article 9, which Myanmar had accepted, and ruled that the Gambia had the right to submit a case to the ICJ.
The ICJ also rejected the second objection by the Myanmar side, that the Gambia was not a country directly involved in the Rohingya crisis and therefore did not have the right to participate in the case. The ICJ ruled that any state party to the Genocide Convention, which protects against crimes against humanity, has the right to bring a case against another state party to the Convention. The decision was supported by 15 judges, with one dissenting.
In the end, the ICJ rejected all Myanmar objections and ruled that the Gambian case against Myanmar, alleging genocide against the Rohingya, will continue. Details of the ruling will be published soon, and it did not specify when the hearings will resume.

◇ SMR (Small Modular Reactor) is a small nuclear reactor, which can produce electricity from 20 megawatts to 300 megawatts depending on its size. 300 megawatts is only one-third of the capacity of a regular nuclear power plant. An SMR reactor is a type of reactor that can be built in one place, assembled in parts, transported to the place where it will be used, and then assembled and used in a short time.

◇ The SMR reactor uses light water as a coolant. Like a conventional nuclear reactor, a small SMR reactor uses heat energy to drive a steam turbine and generator to produce electricity. 👁 What is a squint
A squint is a condition in which the muscles that control the eyes in both eyes do not work together. In other words, the two eyes are divided and each is the master of the other. While the good eye can look straight ahead, the squinting eye is either up, inward, down, or outward.
Squint is an interesting eye condition that you may have seen and experienced in your own life, so let's read on. 
.
👁 Why do you have a squint? 
🔷 Congenital squint
🔷 Family history of squint
🔷 Damage to the brain and cranial nerves 
🔷 When a child has farsightedness, they have to adjust their eyes to see clearly. 
🔷 Measles, diseases such as hydrocephalus, which is a condition that causes increased pressure in the brain and skull, and genetic diseases such as Down's Syndrome and cerebral palsy, can also cause squint. 
.
👁 A point to note
In infants under (3) months of age, squint is not a cause for concern because it usually goes away on its own. If the squint persists after (3) months of age, it can be considered abnormal and should be treated because it does not go away on its own. 
.
👁 In what situations should I consult a doctor?
▪️If the squint does not go away on its own and is persistent
▪️If the baby continues to squint after (3) months of age
▪️If one eye is closed and the other is used to focus
▪️If the head is tilted when focusing
▪️If there is a double vision in the retina 
▪️If the squint is not congenital but develops in adulthood 
(Or) if the squint is accompanied by frequent headaches or vomiting……. 
You should see an ophthalmologist and receive the necessary treatment. 
.
👁 Complications of squint
If the squint is left untreated…
▪️Blurred vision, double vision in the retina 
▪️Lazy eye that does not work anymore 
Lazy eye is a condition in which the brain does not recognize the visual stimuli (input) sent to the brain from the squinting eye and does not work to form an image. Therefore, the squinting eye becomes lazy eye because it does not work much. The good eye on the other side can use its own power to increase its power. 
(In this case... Cover the good eye that is working more with a cloth (or) a bandage and ask the lazy eye to work more. Ask it to focus on it. This way, you can retrain it to relieve the lazy eye.)
▪️Squinting can cause low self-confidence, low self-esteem, and being teased by peers. 
.
👁 Treatments for squinting are... 

squinting is more effective if it is detected and treated early in life. 
▪️If squinting is caused by nearsightedness/farsightedness, prescription glasses with the right power will help.
▪️ Some injections that weaken the eye muscles (such as Botulinum injections) can also help correct a squinting eye.
▪️ Eye exercises are not a cure, but they can be beneficial. 
Here are some examples of eye exercises for squinting:

(✏️Hold a pencil in front of your face, directly in front of your eyes. Gradually move your nose forward until you see a single pencil image. Continue moving your nose forward until you see a single pencil image. Then... try moving your nose forward until you see a single image again. If you can't see a single image again, start the exercise from the beginning.) 
▪️ Squint surgery can also be performed for squint. The surgery can be performed at any age, but it is said to be more effective in children up to 6 years old.
………
Squint is a different body shape and appearance, so don't be discouraged. Don't be discouraged. Accept your eyes as unique and different from others. 
See an eye doctor and get treatment.

 The Republic of the Union of Myanmar welcomes the interactive dialogue with the High Commissioner for Human Rights on Myanmar, as well as OHCHR's corresponding report on the 'Situation of human rights in Myanmar since 1 February 2022'. 
 High Commissioner Türk was blunt in telling the Human Rights Council that "[t]he disregard and contempt for human life and human rights that are continuously demonstrated by the military constitute an outrage to the conscience of humanity." 
 OHCHR has also delivered a strong report on the 'catastrophic' human rights situation in Myanmar and the illegal military junta's grave human rights violations and probable crimes against humanity and war crimes. Further, its report catalogs some of the constructive actions taken by the National Unity Government consistent with Myanmar's international obligations.
 OHCHR's collective updates are strikingly familiar in their content and findings. Each periodic report since the junta's failed power grab in 2021 has recorded fresh peaks in murders, executions, disappearances, torture, sexual violence, and the junta's blocking of humanitarian aid and use of forced displacement and starvation as tactics of war. 
 Emboldened by 'continuous and absolute impunity', the junta has intensified its use of heavy weapons against civilians over the past year. According to High Commissioner Türk, airstrikes against civilian locations increased by 141% and artillery shelling of communities, including hospitals, schools and places of worship, increased by over 100%. 
 OHCHR has also documented clear junta acts of terror and collective punishment, including villagers being burned alive, the hostage-taking of children, and a 1,200% increase in houses burned or destroyed in junta operations. Significantly, OHCHR attributes these widespread and systematic atrocities to the junta's leadership:
 OHCHR documented consistent tactics and patterns of abuse across the country confirming that the military operates as a solid and coherent structure, implying knowledge of its leadership's commission of atrocities and/or, at least, failures to foreseeably prevent them. 
 Accountability is essential. On behalf of Myanmar, the National Unity Government welcomes OHCHR's call for the Security Council to refer the situation in the country to the International Criminal Court (ICC), as well as its acknowledgment that no public response has yet been issued by the ICC to the National Unity Government's July 2021 statement accepting the Court's jurisdiction for crimes committed in Myanmar since 1 July 2002. 
 Furthermore, there has been no discernible improvement in the lives of the Rohingya despite the generosity of Myanmar's neighbors. The Rohingya are no closer to returning home, with OHCHR reporting that conditions in Rakhine State remain unconducive for safe returns and that persistent security concerns have worsened. Yet this situation does not remove the National Unity Government's responsibility to the Rohingya, including much needed progress on citizenship rights. We stand by these commitments. 
 The National Unity Government also accepts OHCHR's calls on all parties to adhere to their international obligations, to ensure full, unrestricted, predictable humanitarian access to all persons in need, and to cooperate with international human rights and accountability mechanisms. Further, we support High Commissioner Türk's treaty that all parties strengthen their efforts to ensure civilian protection.

Finally, the National Unity Government fully endorses the High Commissioner's call on the Council to respect the democratic will of the Myanmar people. To High Commissioner Türk:

 The Republic of the Union of Myanmar welcomes the Human Rights Council's adoption by consensus of the resolution on the situation of human rights in Myanmar. Myanmar extends its appreciation to the European Union and to cosponsors. 
 The new resolution is stronger than last year's text and it capitalises on recent momentum, including the UN Security Council's historic 2022 resolution on Myanmar which stressed the need to uphold democratic institutions and processes in Myanmar in accordance with the will of the people. As the Human Rights Council's new resolution confirms, the Myanmar people expressed this democratic will in the general election held on 8 November 2020. 
 The new resolution also condemns the illegal military junta's deliberate, widespread, indiscriminate and disproportionate use of force against civilians, including airstrikes, killings, torture and sexual and gender-based violence. This established pattern of intentional attacks constitutes likely crimes against humanity in addition to certain war crimes and grave human rights violations and abuses.

 The junta's atrocities also demand accountability. The new resolution expresses strong support for accountability processes, including at the International Court of Justice and through the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar's (IIMM) preparation of case files. Progress must see the International Criminal Court (ICC) recognize the National Unity Government's article 12(3) declaration issued in July 2021, which accepted the ICC's jurisdiction over international crimes committed in Myanmar since 1 July 2002.
 Significantly, the new resolution welcomes the National Unity Government's pronouncement of its "Policy position on the Rohingya in Rakhine State" on 3 June 2021. The Republic of the Union of Myanmar, as represented by the National Unity Government, recognizes the Rohingya as Myanmar citizens and remains committed to replacing the 1982 Citizenship Law and to the voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return of Rohingya refugees to their homes in Myanmar.
 On ASEAN, the resolution supports the regional group's efforts while expressing deep concern at the lack of progress in implementing the Five-Point Consensus. Accordingly, the Human Rights Council has requested the UN Secretary-General to continue to call the Security Council's attention to the situation in Myanmar. The Security Council should in turn consider all measures at its disposal, including those under Chapter VII of the UN Charter given the threat that the junta poses to peace and security.
 The resolution also invites the Secretary-General to 'offer relevant recommendations to enable more effective work in the future and to strengthen the prevention capacity of the United Nations system' in follow-up to the Rosenthal report. Acting on this invitation, the Secretary-General should commission an inquiry into whether the UN Country Team in Myanmar is taking adequate steps to avoid a repeat of past UN failures and to meet its obligations under the Secretary-General's Call to Action for Human Rights and under the UNCT's own 'programmatic engagement guidelines'. A public report with clear findings and recommendations should follow.

Myanmar, as represented by the National Unity Government, supports the Human Rights Council's extension of the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Myanmar and accepts the call for an OHCHR country office to be opened. Myanmar will also continue to cooperate with the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General on Myanmar, the IIMM and other UN mandate-holders, human rights mechanisms and international and regional courts, tribunals and human rights bodies.

Dr. Sasa's Message on the 47th Anniversary of the Hanging of Myanmar's Student Leader, Salai Tin Maung Oo, for Anti-Military Dictatorship on June 26, 1976:
 
 26 June 2023
 
 Salai Tin Maung Oo's famous saying was, "They can kill my body but not my beliefs."
 On this day in 1976, Salai Tin Maung Oo, a 25-year-old student leader, was brutally executed by hanging in Insein Prison. His execution marked one of the darkest chapters in Myanmar's struggle for inclusive federal democracy. Salai Tin Maung Oo's only "crime" was expressing his belief in federal democracy and his opposition to genocidal military dictatorships. He shared famous proverbs and wisdom that resonated with the people of Myanmar who sought freedom and federal democracy. Born on June 11, 1951, in Taungoo, Myanmar, Salai Tin Maung Oo was a beacon of hope for many during a challenging period in Myanmar's history.
 At the young age of 11, Salai Tin Maung Oo witnessed the coup that took place in 1962, marking the beginning of a tumultuous era in his country. At the age of 21, Salai Tin Maung Oo was unlawfully arrested by genocidal military general Ne Win on December 5, 1972, for advocating federal democratic principles. After enduring brutal conditions, he was released from prison on January 3, 1974. He played a significant role in advocating for the use of "Salai" before Chin male names and "Mai" before Chin female names for the Chin people of Myanmar.
 During the Burma crisis in 1974, known as U Thant's crisis, Salai Tin Maung Oo emerged as a prominent figure at the age of 23. U Thant, a Burmese diplomat, served as the third Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1961 to 1971. Salai Tin Maung Oo, an ethnic Chin zoological student at the University of Yangon, participated in student movements and labor strikes against military rule. He gained recognition in 1974 when students protested against brutal military dictator Ne Win's refusal to grant a state funeral to former United Nations secretary-general U Thant, who had passed away that year.
 Tragically, on March 19, 1976, Salai Tin Maung Oo was unjustly rearrested along with his father, U Mya Din, his brother, Salai Hla Swe, and his sister, Mai Po Po, who actively participated in the struggle for freedom and federal democracy by the brutal military dictator Ne Win due to his unwavering struggle for freedom and federal democracy. He bravely prolonged his last breath as a symbol of his final struggle for Myanmar's freedom and federal democracy. His courageous spirit represented the true essence of the brave people of Myanmar. We pledge our cooperation with international, regional and national accountability mechanisms, particularly countries exercising universal jurisdiction. This builds on our article 12(3) declaration to the International Criminal Court in 2021, which accepted the Court's jurisdiction in Myanmar going back to 1 July 2002.

We strongly support the IIMM's efforts to hold the military accountable for its atrocity campaigns against the Rohingya, and we are ready to explore the IIMM's access to Myanmar to facilitate on the ground investigations into the military junta's widespread crimes.

The Union Minister, as well as NUG representative for France Nan Su Mon Aung and advisor to the Ministry of Human Rights U Jaivet Ealom, attended the occasion.
 In the briefing, the Union Minister discussed Myanmar's human rights challenges, territory control conditions, the advancement of ethnic organizations and democratic alliances, civil administration, and law enforcement procedures. 
 He also requested 5 points for the international community and 3 points for the Council as follows: 
 Firstly, the International Community 
 1. Block the flow of arms, munitions, cash and jet fuel to the junta through global coordinated sanctions. Starve the junta of its capacity to murder civilians.
 2. Recognize and directly engage with the NUG and its ethnic partners, and provide us with increased financial, technical, material and humanitarian assistance – including through cross-border channels. 
 3. Push for resumed Security Council action on Myanmar. It has been 15 months since the adoption of resolution 2669 on Myanmar. The junta has ignored every one of its demands.
 4. Reject any attempts by the junta to launch a negotiated settlement as a lifeline. Now is when the cycle of Myanmar dictatorship ends. The armed forces must be made permanently subordinate to a democratic civilian government. 
 5. Put constructive pressure on the UN. The UN Special Envoy post has been vacant since last June and the role of Resident Coordinator in Myanmar is back to rotating between UN agency heads. This lack of structure and hierarchy risks competing priorities, and shows a dangerous lack of vision. 
 And here are 3 steps the HRC can take in its HRC55 Myanmar text:

1. Be creative in exploring accountability options. This could include requesting OHCHR to prepare a report on accountability options for Myanmar, like it has been asked to do on Afghanistan and Sri Lanka. This would build on OHCHR's comprehensive documentation of violations and abuses, and help put the IIMM's case files to use.
 2. Request the Secretary-General to prepare an updated report on what the UNCT in Myanmar is doing to implement the Rosenthal report's recommendations and to strengthen the UN's prevention capacity. 
 3. Strengthen your references to the National Unity Government and its ethnic partners, and strengthen your condemnation of the military junta's atrocities. Make it absolutely clear that, in the eyes of this Council, the junta has no legitimacy, no authority, and no future.

Today is International Mine Awareness Day, which is celebrated every year on April 4 in various countries around the world. April 4 was designated by the United Nations on December 8, 2005 as International Mine Awareness Day to raise awareness and raise awareness about landmines, explosive remnants of war, and bombs. 

This year, with the theme “Protecting Lives, Building Peace,” we have identified the following objectives: to prevent the loss of life by clearing landmines, to contribute to the development of societies by clearing landmines, and to raise awareness of countries that are still at risk of landmines.

Myanmar is one of the few countries in the world that still produces and uses landmines. More than half of the townships in Myanmar are covered in landmines, and the number is increasing. The illegal takeover by the military junta has caused significant civilian casualties, and the loss of innocent lives due to landmines is also a contributing factor.

The relevant ministries of our National Unity Government are also working with local public administrations, civil defense organizations, and humanitarian agencies to reduce the impact on innocent civilians by organizing awareness-raising lectures, distributing pamphlets, and distributing mine safety brochures.

As long as the military dictatorship in Myanmar continues, people will continue to suffer from landmines. Only by ending the military dictatorship as soon as possible and establishing the federal democratic union that the people desire, can we achieve lasting peace and establish a safe and prosperous society. Therefore, we urge everyone to participate in the International Mine Awareness Day 2024, which falls today.

Ultraviolet Radiation and Your Health (April 2024)

🔴 Key points

☀️ Skin cancers are caused primarily by exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the sun or from man-made sources such as sunbeds. 
☀️ In 2020, more than 1.5 million new cases of skin cancer were diagnosed worldwide, and more than 120,000 people died.
☀️ 15 million people worldwide are blind due to cataracts, and 10% of these people may be affected by UV exposure.
☀️ Excessive sun exposure in children and adolescents is associated with skin cancer later in life.
☀️ To a certain extent, UV exposure provides health benefits, such as providing vitamin D.
☀️ There are simple and effective ways to prevent skin cancer. It is recommended to avoid sun exposure with a UV index of 3 or higher.

🔴 Overview

UV radiation is invisible. It is not felt. Some people are exposed to man-made UV rays (e.g., from pharmaceuticals, factories, cosmetics, and pesticides), and everyone is exposed to UV rays from the sun.

The amount of UV rays from the sun is affected by many factors.

☀️ Altitude - The higher the altitude, the higher the amount of UV rays. UV rays vary throughout the day and year.

☀️ Latitude - The closer to the equator, the higher the amount of UV rays.

☀️ Altitude - The higher the altitude above sea level, the thinner the air and the less UV rays it absorbs.

☀️ Cloud cover - UV rays are highest when there are no clouds, but they can be higher when there are clouds.

☀️ Ozone - The ozone layer absorbs some of the sun's UV rays. A thin ozone layer allows more UV rays to reach the Earth's surface.
☀️ Reflection - Reflective surfaces such as water, sand, and snow increase the amount of UV radiation.
☀️ Climate change, including changes in the ozone layer and cloud cover, is thought to affect the amount of UV radiation on Earth.

🔴 Health effects

Small amounts of UV radiation play an important role in the production of vitamin D and are beneficial for health. However, excessive exposure to UV radiation has been linked to adverse health effects, such as cancer.

☀️ Effects on the skin

The most common effects of UV radiation include DNA damage, sunburn, skin irritation, allergies, and a weakened immune system. A weakened immune system can be a risk factor for cancer and can lead to the resurgence of viruses. (Example: Lip ulcers)

Long-term effects of UV exposure on the skin and lips

👉 Cutaneous melanoma - a life-threatening type of skin cancer
👉 Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) - a type of skin cancer that is generally less common and less deadly than melanoma
👉 Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) - a slow-growing type of skin cancer that is more common in older people
👉 Premature skin aging - the loss of skin elasticity at a young age and slow healing

In 2020, excessive UV exposure was estimated to cause 1.2 million new cases of SCC and BCC, 325,000 new cases of melanoma, and 64,000 premature deaths from SCC and BCC, and 57,000 from melanoma.

☀️ Effects on the eyes

The most common side effects of UV rays include photokeratitis and photoconjunctivitis. These effects are reversible and can be easily prevented with protective eyewear. Long-term damage is unlikely, but they can be painful and require treatment.

Long-term effects of UV rays include:

👉 Cataracts (an eye disease in which the lens in the eye becomes increasingly cloudy, causing vision loss and eventually blindness),
👉 Pterygium (a growth of tissue that can cover part of the cornea),
👉 Cancers in and around the eye (BCC, SCC, and melanoma).

UV exposure can also contribute to age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

It is estimated that there are approximately 15 million people worldwide who lose their vision due to cataracts, and about 10 percent of these are due to UV exposure.

☀️ Vitamin D Production

Small amounts of UV light are important for good health because they are essential for the body’s production of vitamin D. Vitamin D helps strengthen the bones and muscles. People who do not get enough sun exposure should consider taking a vitamin D supplement. People with low sun exposure include those living in care homes or confined to their homes, those with darker skin in high altitudes, and those who wear full-body coverings when outdoors due to religious or traditional beliefs.

🔴 People at particular risk

Children and adolescents are more susceptible to UV damage because of the structure of their skin and eyes. Sunburns in childhood increase the risk of skin cancer later in life. High levels of UV radiation can also reach the retina and damage it.

Fair-skinned people are more susceptible to sunburn and skin cancer than dark-skinned people. However, dark-skinned people can also get skin cancer. Eye damage is important for everyone. 

People at higher risk of skin cancer include those with multiple birthmarks/moles, those receiving photosensitive treatments, and those with a family history of skin cancer. People who work outdoors and are exposed to UV radiation from the sun are at higher risk of SCC and BCC skin cancers.

🔴 Prevention methods

Skin cancer can be prevented effectively. The World Health Organization recommends the following to protect against excessive exposure to UV rays:

☀️ Avoid the sun during the middle of the day as much as possible.

☀️ Stay in the shade.

☀️ Wear clothing that protects against direct sunlight.

☀️ Wear a wide-brimmed hat to protect your eyes, face, ears, and neck.
☀️ Wear sunglasses that block 99 to 100 percent of UV-A and UV-B rays.
☀️ Apply an effective sunscreen to areas of your skin that are not covered by clothing. The best way to protect yourself from the sun is to seek shade and wear clothing. Sunscreen should not be used for prolonged exposure to the sun.
☀️ Avoid tanning beds and machines. Using sunbeds to expose yourself to ultraviolet rays increases the risk of skin cancer. These methods should never be considered a substitute for getting enough vitamin D. 

By ensuring that children use the simple precautions listed above when playing outdoors, you can prevent both short-term and long-term damage.

Ministry of Health, Government of National Unity

 The Republic of the Union of Myanmar, as represented by the National Unity Government, welcomes the interactive dialogue on Myanmar with the Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as OHCHR's corresponding report on the human rights situation in Myanmar.
  
 In the words of Deputy High Commissioner Nada Al-Nashif, "Myanmar continues to sink into an abyss of human suffering". The Deputy High Commissioner cataloged before the Council a range of military junta atrocities – airstrikes and artillery attacks as “weapons of choice” against civilians; the manipulation of humanitarian aid, seen yet again in the aftermath of Cyclone Yagi; the deliberate destruction of Myanmar youth through a campaign of forced conscription; and the "rampant" use of torture and sexual violence against women and LBGTI persons in arbitrary detention.
  
 OHCHR's latest report on Myanmar (A/HRC/57/56) explores these same crimes in detail. It also addresses the grave situation in northern Rakhine State, where horrific reports and images have emerged from Maungdaw township and surrounding areas. This raises the alarm about potential new atrocities against the Rohingya, the Rakhine, and other minority communities. The Republic of the Union of Myanmar, as represented by the National Unity Government, is fully committed to preventing such crimes and to ensuring that shameful past failures in Myanmar are never repeated.
  
 Deputy High Commissioner Al-Nashif also repeated earlier OHCHR calls on UN Member States and ASEAN Members to adopt a "new approach" to end the junta-induced crisis in Myanmar. Three steps were proposed, each of which Myanmar supports:
  
 1. Concrete action to block the flow of arms, other military material and aviation fuel to the junta. This must be done through a new Security Council resolution in follow-up to resolution 2669 (2022) that also formally places Myanmar on the Council's agenda through regular reporting.
  
 2. A renewed political process through direct engagement with the National Unity Government, ethnic armed groups, civil society, women and young people to define future solutions for Myanmar
  
 3. Finding creative ways to get humanitarian aid to all communities in need, including through cross-border operations and established ethnic, civil society and community-based organizations. Myanmar, however, cautions the international community against cooperating with the military junta, which continues to manipulate and withhold humanitarian aid as a tactic of war.
  
 Myanmar further supports the Deputy High Commissioner's calls for accountability, including through a Security Council referral of the situation in Myanmar to the ICC. We remain committed to cooperating with the ICJ and national jurisdictions to advance justice and reparations. And we will continue to work with OHCHR, the IIMM and the Special Rapporteur on Myanmar to secure meaningful access to Myanmar to facilitate investigations, monitoring and reporting on the human rights situation.
  
 Finally, Myanmar wholly accepts OHCHR's call on the National Unity Government to fully respect international humanitarian law and human rights, including by holding perpetrators of violations accountable, in accordance with international standards. We hold ourselves to this standard and expect the same of all actors in Myanmar.
  
 In closing, Myanmar remains deeply grateful to High Commissioner Türk, Deputy High Commissioner Al-Nashif and to OHCHR's Myanmar Team for their continued efforts to expose the military junta's atrocities and to push the world to act.

 Myanmar associates itself with the statement delivered by NAM.

Statement by Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun, Permanent Representative of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar to the United Nations, at the General Discussion on Social Development of the Third Committee of the Seventy-Ninth session of the UN General Assembly (New York, 4 October 2024)

Mr. Chair,

I wish to extend our warmest congratulations to you and the bureau for your well-deserved elections. Please be assured of our delegation's full support and cooperation in your work.
 
 Myanmar aligns itself with the statements by ASEAN and G-77 and China.
 
 This year, UN member states mark the historic success of adopting the Pact for the Future. Myanmar is of the view that the Pact serves as a key driver and testifies the ultimate ambition to reverse stagnation and keep the world on track for the implementation of SDGs and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
 
 However, the global community is still deeply rooted in the cycle of challenges resulting from the ongoing conflicts, military coups and natural disasters which are threatening and impeding international peace, security and solidarity.
 
 More needs to be done through an effective multilateral system.
 
 In this regard, Myanmar thanks the UN Secretary-General for his reports under this agenda item and welcomes his recommendations contained therein.
 
 Mr. Chair,
 
 Very sadly, in my country Myanmar, since the illegal military coup attempt in February 2021, the perpetrating military junta has been consistently committing series of atrocities in a systematic and widespread manner by launching indiscriminate aerial bombings on the civilian population and destroying and burning down villages and civilian properties.
 
 The whole people of Myanmar especially women and girls, children, persons with disabilities, and youth are bearing the brunt of the military dictatorship and its atrocities.
 
 Since the coup attempt in February 2021, over 5,700 people have been brutally killed by the military junta. More than 3.4 million people are displaced. Over 18.6 million people are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.
 
 More than half of those in need of humanitarian assistance are women and girls.

They are disproportionately affected by unemployment and gender-specific impacts including increasing vulnerability to gender-based violence, rape, sexual exploitation and harassment, lack of access to essential services for responding, preventing, and documenting violence against women due to displacements, security risks, and damage to infrastructure and increased gender-based crimes such as trafficking.
 
 Even at this challenging time, women are at the forefront in fighting against the military dictatorship and restoring democracy in Myanmar.
 
 Mr. Chair,
 
 Over 6 million children have been part of the displacement and living under interrupted health-care and formal education. In some cases, some children are pursuing education in makeshift camps and bunkers due to the junta's aerial attacks and heavy artillery shelling. They are also facing food insecurity and malnutrition due to lack of access to regular immunization and vaccination. Underage children are also at risk of forced recruitment by the military.
 
 I also wish to stress that persons with disabilities especially women suffer the most. Accessibility is getting difficult. Violation of their rights is more frequent. Due to the junta's atrocities, aerial attacks and landmines, many people including women and girls lost part of their body.
 
 Our youth play an important and leading role in our fight for democracy. Although they are supposed to be at classes and universities, many of them joined the revolution against the inhumane military junta to save lives and protect the community. Some left the country to avoid possible arbitrary arrest by the junta. Massive migration and the issue of brain drain have become more alarming after the military junta's forced conscription. 
 
 Unfortunately, the evolution of recent Typhoon Ragi and its remnants have further exacerbated displacement, the people's suffering and the humanitarian situation.
 
 Mr. Chair,
 
 Many countries informed this august committee of how much effort they put to promote social protection of their respective citizens. Sadly in Myanmar, instead of paying attention to the social protection, we are crying out for help to protect civilians from the military junta's atrocities.
 
 Clearly, the root cause of the people's suffering and the crisis in Myanmar is the military dictatorship and its unlawful military coup attempt. We need to end this root cause. The international community needs to step up and take bolder actions to address this destructive root cause.
 
 In this regard, the people of Myanmar have persistently appealed to the international community and the UN, particularly the Security Council, to take effective action to save lives and prevent the junta's atrocities by cutting off arms, weapons, jet fuel and financial supplies to the military junta.
 
 In conclusion, Mr. Chair, I wish to emphasize that free and fair elections are fundamental values ​​of democracy. However, any election to be organized by the military junta in this situation will never be a free, fair and inclusive election. The junta's planned sham election is not a solution for the crisis but rather will create more violence and prolong the conflict.
 
 Therefore the people of Myanmar are resolute, and we strongly oppose the junta's planned sham election. We call for the international community to do the same.
 
 Thank you.

2. Ambassador U Kyaw Moe Htun, Permanent Representative of Myanmar to the United Nations, said on 18-10-2024 (Friday), He delivered his morning address, which included the following key points:

(b) He stressed that the effective implementation of the Secretary-General’s new vision on the rule of law is crucial for the development of peace and stability at the national, regional and international levels;

The military junta has committed war crimes and crimes against humanity, including the brutal killing of more than 5,800 civilians and the displacement of more than 3.4 million people.

The breakdown of the rule of law in Myanmar poses a significant challenge to the sustainability of the international legal order. It undermines international efforts to uphold international human rights standards, weakens the collective capacity of States to uphold and apply international law, and has an impact on the stability and effectiveness of the international rules-based system.

(i) It is therefore highly anticipated that the activities of the United Nations International Investigative Mechanism on Myanmar will contribute to the efforts of the Burmese people to achieve justice for the victims of violence and thereby to the rule of law.

The restoration of the rule of law in Burma depends on the rule of law being governed by a legitimate civilian government that respects the principles of federal democracy and international human rights and humanitarian law.

(l) The international community and the United Nations Security Council must immediately heed the demands of the people of Burma and take concrete and effective measures to restore democracy and the rule of law in the country.
